title: Through the roof (Mark 2:1–12)
hookLine: four friends dig through a roof to lower their paralyzed friend to Jesus

lines: A HOUSE PACKED TO THE DOOR.
NO WAY THROUGH. THEY LOOK UP.
cards: Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake. Word gets around that Jesus is back, staying in a house, and the house fills. Then the doorway.
Then the street outside. Mark says there was no room, not even at the door. Now four men come down the street carrying a mat, and on the mat is their friend.
He can't walk. He can't get himself anywhere. They reach the crowd and stop.
There's no way through. It would be easy to turn around. Maybe tomorrow, when it's quieter.

teach.b: So they climb onto the roof, carrying him, and start digging. Mark says they uncovered the roof, broke it open, and let down the mat.
Imagine being inside: dust and bits of clay falling on everyone, daylight opening in the ceiling, and a man lowered into the middle of the sermon. Now the line to catch.
Mark says: when Jesus saw their faith. The friends'. We don't hear a word from the man on the mat; it's the four who carried him whose trust Jesus sees.
Then Jesus says something nobody expected: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." Some scribes sitting there are troubled, reasoning in their hearts: who can forgive sins but God alone?
Jesus asks them which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk. Then, so they'll know he has that authority, he turns to the man: "Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house."
And he does, in front of everyone, carrying the mat that carried him. The crowd says: we never saw the like. The Church hears two things here.
One is the sacraments of healing, confession and the anointing of the sick, where forgiveness and healing are asked for together.
The other is intercession: carrying someone to God when they can't get there themselves.
That's what Catholics are doing when they pray for each other, and when they ask the saints to pray for them.

how: Catholics pray for one another and ask the saints for their prayers, and the Church offers the sacraments of healing, confession and the anointing of the sick, which the Catechism connects with stories like this one.

o: a woven rug for kneeling to pray
a floor covering at a house's door
a simple bed a sick man was carried on

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Mark says Jesus saw the paralyzed man's faith
Mark says Jesus saw their faith: the friends who carried him.
Jesus forgives the man before he heals him
first “Son, thy sins are forgiven thee,” then, arise, take up thy bed.
the man leaves carrying his own mat

games.q: you and three friends carry a man who can't walk to a house. the crowd blocks the door. what do you do?
o: wait outside until the crowd thins.
climb up and open the roof.
shout until someone lets you in.
games.why: they go up, open the roof and let him down on his mat. Mark says Jesus saw their faith.

practice: Think of one person who can't get where they need to be right now, someone sick, or stuck, or too worn out to ask for help, and picture yourself as one of the four at the corners of the mat.
If you pray, carry them to God in your own words, or with a prayer you know. If you don't, hold them in mind with care, and ask yourself which corner of the mat you could lift this week.

wordCard.voice: mat. What the four friends carried their paralyzed friend on, breaking through a roof to bring him to Jesus.

orig.note: Greek: a mat or pallet, a poor person's bed. Mark's word for what the friends carried.

carryVoice: Your line: friends dig through roofs. Jesus saw the faith of the ones carrying. See you tomorrow.
